content_html:
Many Muslim parents look for daily duas for kids that are short, authentic and easy for little ones to remember. The good news is that the Sunnah is full of adhkar that are just one word or one sentence long, which even a three-year-old can say. In this guide we gather the most important daily adhkar for children with their sources, explain their meanings in child-friendly words, and suggest a daily routine plus games and rewards that turn remembrance of Allah into a habit your child loves.

What are the best short daily duas for kids?

  1. Waking up: "Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi ahyana ba'da ma amatana wa ilayhin-nushur."
  2. Before eating: "Bismillah." After eating: "Alhamdulillah."
  3. Entering the toilet: "Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-khubuthi wal-khaba'ith."
  4. Leaving home: "Bismillah, tawakkaltu 'alallah."
  5. After sneezing: "Alhamdulillah."
  6. Morning and evening: Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq and An-Nas, three times each.
  7. Before sleep: "Bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya."

These seven are a strong starting core, and each one is established in the Sunnah, as we show below with its source. Start with two or three, then add one new dhikr each week until the whole day is covered.

Why teach children adhkar from a young age?

Dhikr connects a child's heart to Allah in every part of the day: when they eat, dress, go out and sleep. Allah says:

﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَتَطْمَئِنُّ قُلُوبُهُم بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ ۗ أَلَا بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ﴾
"Those who have believed and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allah. Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts are assured." [Surah Ar-Ra'd 13:28, Sahih International]

Children need that reassurance more than anyone. When they are scared of the dark or anxious at bedtime, dhikr gives them a sense of safety. The Prophet ﷺ taught children directly. He said to 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah, who was a young boy at the time:

«يَا غُلَامُ، سَمِّ اللَّهَ، وَكُلْ بِيَمِينِكَ، وَكُلْ مِمَّا يَلِيكَ»
Meaning: "Young boy, say Allah's name, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is in front of you." (Sahih al-Bukhari 5376, Sahih Muslim 2022)

Notice the Prophet's method: a kind call, "young boy", then three short, clear instructions, with no telling-off. That is the approach we want when teaching our own children. He ﷺ also said to the young Ibn 'Abbas: "Young man, I will teach you some words: be mindful of Allah and He will protect you" (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2516, graded hasan sahih by at-Tirmidhi). To learn more about the virtues of remembrance in general, read our article on the virtues of morning and evening adhkar.

Kids' adhkar from waking up to bedtime, with simple explanations

We arrange the adhkar here around a child's day. Each one comes with a simple explanation you can tell your child in your own words. Arabic is given first, then transliteration and meaning.

1. When waking up

«الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي أَحْيَانَا بَعْدَ مَا أَمَاتَنَا وَإِلَيْهِ النُّشُورُ»
Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi ahyana ba'da ma amatana wa ilayhin-nushur.
Meaning: "All praise is for Allah, who gave us life after causing us to die, and to Him is the return." (Reported by al-Bukhari)

For your child: Sleep is like a little death, and Allah brought us back to life so we can play and learn again. So we thank Him the moment we open our eyes.

2. Entering and leaving the toilet

Entering: «اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنَ الْخُبُثِ وَالْخَبَائِثِ» Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-khubuthi wal-khaba'ith. Meaning: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the male and female devils." (Sahih al-Bukhari 142, Sahih Muslim 375)
Leaving: «غُفْرَانَكَ» Ghufranak. Meaning: "I ask Your forgiveness." (Reported by Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi)

For your child: We ask Allah to protect us from the shayatin in this place. We go in with the left foot and come out with the right.

3. When getting dressed

«الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي كَسَانِي هَذَا وَرَزَقَنِيهِ مِنْ غَيْرِ حَوْلٍ مِنِّي وَلَا قُوَّةٍ»
Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi kasani hadha wa razaqanihi min ghayri hawlin minni wa la quwwah.
Meaning: "All praise is for Allah who clothed me with this and provided it for me without any power or strength from me." (Reported by Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi)

For your child: Your clothes are a gift from Allah. A very young child can start with just "Alhamdulillah" and learn the full wording later.

4. Eating adhkar

  • Before eating: "Bismillah" (In the name of Allah).
  • If they forget at the start: "Bismillahi awwalahu wa akhirah" (In the name of Allah at its beginning and its end), reported by Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi.
  • After eating: "Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi at'amani hadha wa razaqanihi min ghayri hawlin minni wa la quwwah" (All praise is for Allah who fed me this and provided it for me without any power or strength from me), reported by Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi.

For your child: When we say "Bismillah", Allah puts blessing in our food. When we say "Alhamdulillah", we thank Him for it. Teach the manners of eating with the right hand and from what is in front of you alongside the words, as in the hadith of 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah.

5. Leaving and entering the home

«بِسْمِ اللَّهِ، تَوَكَّلْتُ عَلَى اللَّهِ، وَلَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ»
Bismillah, tawakkaltu 'alallah, wa la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah.
Meaning: "In the name of Allah, I place my trust in Allah, and there is no might nor power except with Allah." (Reported by Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi)

When coming home, we mention Allah. The Prophet ﷺ said that when a person enters their home and mentions Allah on entering and when eating, Shaytan says to his companions: "There is no place for you to stay tonight and no dinner" (Sahih Muslim 2018).

For your child: When we remember Allah at the door and at dinner, Shaytan finds no bed in our house and no food at our table. Children love this picture and remember it.

6. When getting in the car

﴿سُبْحَانَ الَّذِي سَخَّرَ لَنَا هَٰذَا وَمَا كُنَّا لَهُ مُقْرِنِينَ ۝ وَإِنَّا إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ﴾
"Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have [otherwise] subdued it. And indeed we, to our Lord, will [surely] return." [Surah Az-Zukhruf 43:13–14, Sahih International]

For your child: We could never make something that carries us so fast on our own. Allah made the car easy for us, so we glorify and thank Him. Let your child be the "trip reminder" who says it out loud when the car sets off.

7. When sneezing

The Prophet ﷺ said: "When one of you sneezes, let him say 'Alhamdulillah', and let his brother or companion say to him 'Yarhamukallah' (may Allah have mercy on you). When he says 'Yarhamukallah', let him reply 'Yahdikumullahu wa yuslihu balakum' (may Allah guide you and set your affairs right)." (Sahih al-Bukhari 6224)

For your child: This is a dhikr the whole family says to each other, and kids find it one of the most fun because it happens suddenly and needs a quick reply.

8. When hearing the adhan

The Prophet ﷺ said: "When you hear the call, say what the mu'adhdhin says" (Sahih al-Bukhari 611, Sahih Muslim 383). Teach your child to pause their game for a moment and repeat after the mu'adhdhin. It is a beautiful first step toward prayer, which we cover in detail in how to teach kids to pray.

9. When angry

Two men argued in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ and one became very angry. The Prophet ﷺ said he knew a phrase that, if the man said it, his anger would leave him: "A'udhu billahi minash-shaytanir-rajim" (I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan). The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim. Teach your child to say it when they are upset with a sibling, then to sit down or drink some water.

Which morning and evening adhkar suit children?

The full morning and evening adhkar are long, and children do not need to read all of them. Choose the short, authentic ones:

  • Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq and An-Nas, three times each, morning and evening. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Say Qul huwa Allahu ahad and the two surahs of refuge in the evening and in the morning three times; they will suffice you against everything" (reported by Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi).
  • «بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الَّذِي لَا يَضُرُّ مَعَ اسْمِهِ شَيْءٌ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِي السَّمَاءِ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ» Bismillahil-ladhi la yadurru ma'asmihi shay'un fil-ardi wa la fis-sama'i wa huwas-Sami'ul-'Alim, three times. Meaning: "In the name of Allah, with whose name nothing on earth or in heaven can cause harm, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing" (reported by Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi).
  • «رَضِيتُ بِاللَّهِ رَبًّا، وَبِالْإِسْلَامِ دِينًا، وَبِمُحَمَّدٍ ﷺ نَبِيًّا» Raditu billahi Rabba, wa bil-Islami dina, wa bi-Muhammadin ﷺ nabiyya, three times. Meaning: "I am pleased with Allah as my Lord, Islam as my religion and Muhammad ﷺ as my Prophet" (reported by Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi).
  • "Subhanallahi wa bihamdih": the Prophet ﷺ said: "Two words are light on the tongue, heavy on the Scale and beloved to the Most Merciful: Subhanallahi wa bihamdihi, Subhanallahil-'Adhim" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim).

The Prophet ﷺ himself used to seek protection for his grandsons al-Hasan and al-Husayn with these words: «أُعِيذُكُمَا بِكَلِمَاتِ اللَّهِ التَّامَّةِ، مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْطَانٍ وَهَامَّةٍ، وَمِنْ كُلِّ عَيْنٍ لَامَّةٍ» "I seek protection for you both in the perfect words of Allah from every devil and every poisonous creature, and from every harmful evil eye" (Sahih al-Bukhari 3371). Parents can say it over their children; for one child, say "U'idhuka" instead of "U'idhukuma".

The Rafiq Al-Taa app has a morning and evening adhkar section with a counter for repetitions. Read together with your child and let them tap the counter themselves so they feel part of it. The app also includes the full Hisn al-Muslim if you want to check the wording of any dhikr.

Bedtime duas for kids

Bedtime is one of the calmest moments of the day and the best time for dhikr, because children listen closely then:

  1. «بِاسْمِكَ اللَّهُمَّ أَمُوتُ وَأَحْيَا» Bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya. Meaning: "In Your name, O Allah, I die and I live" (reported by al-Bukhari).
  2. Ayat al-Kursi: Sahih al-Bukhari reports that whoever recites it when going to bed will have a guardian from Allah, and no devil will come near them until morning.
  3. Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq and An-Nas: when the Prophet ﷺ went to bed, he would cup his hands, blow lightly into them, recite these three surahs and then wipe over as much of his body as he could. This is in Sahih al-Bukhari. A parent can do the same and gently wipe over a young child.

For your child: When we sleep with Allah's name, Allah protects us all night, so there is no need to be afraid of the dark. This idea really helps children who feel scared at bedtime.

A simple daily adhkar routine for children

This table links each dhikr to a fixed moment in your child's day. That link is the secret to consistency:

TimeDhikrLinked habit
Waking upAlhamdu lillahil-ladhi ahyana...Before getting out of bed
BathroomEntering dua, and "Ghufranak" on leavingAt the door
Getting dressedAlhamdu lillahil-ladhi kasani hadha...After putting on school clothes
Breakfast and every mealBismillah before, Alhamdulillah afterBefore the first bite and after the last
Leaving for schoolBismillah, tawakkaltu 'alallah...At the front door
On the roadThe travel dhikrWhen the car or bus moves off
After 'Asr or MaghribThe three Quls three times, and Bismillahil-ladhi la yadurru...A short family circle
BedtimeBismika Allahumma..., Ayat al-Kursi, the three QulsAfter the lights go off

Print this table and hang it in your child's room, or fold it into a family worship chart, as we describe in our daily worship tracker guide.

How to help your child memorize adhkar by age

Ages 3 to 5

Focus on single words and short phrases: "Bismillah", "Alhamdulillah", "Subhanallah", "A'udhu billah". Say them out loud in front of your child at every chance, and they will start repeating them on their own. Don't ask them to memorize; just let them hear.

Ages 6 to 8

This is the age of fast memorization. Add one full dhikr each week, starting with waking, sleeping and eating. Explain the meaning in one sentence and ask questions: "Why do we say Alhamdulillah after eating?"

Ages 9 to 12

Your child can now read adhkar by themselves from a book or app and keep up the short morning and evening adhkar. Give them responsibility: reminding younger siblings, or leading the family dhikr circle once a week.

Games and rewards that make kids love dhikr

  • "What do we say?": name a situation, such as "Your brother sneezed", "We're leaving the house" or "We got in the car", and your child answers with the right dhikr.
  • Picture cards: each card shows a situation (a bed, food, a door) with the dhikr on the back. Use them for a matching game.
  • The dhikr tree: draw a tree on a big sheet of paper and add a green leaf to a branch every time your child learns a new dhikr.
  • The little reminder: make your child responsible for reminding the family of one dhikr, like the travel dua. This role fixes it in memory better than any amount of repetition.
  • Counting on fingers: teach them to count tasbih on their fingers. The Sunnah encourages counting tasbih on the fingertips, and it turns dhikr into a fun physical activity.
  • A gentle chant: some kids memorize best with rhythm. Repeat the short adhkar with a calm tune, without changing any of the words.

About rewards: a simple sticker or star helps at the start, but the most powerful thing is sincere praise and connecting the dhikr to its meaning: "Allah loves those who remember Him, and He said: ﴿فَاذْكُرُونِي أَذْكُرْكُمْ﴾ 'So remember Me; I will remember you' [Surah Al-Baqarah 2:152, Sahih International]." Reduce material rewards gradually so dhikr becomes a habit that comes from the heart.

How do I make dhikr a family habit?

Children love what the family does together. Set aside a short circle of no more than ten minutes, after Maghrib or before bed, where the family reads the three Quls three times, says some tasbih and reviews the dhikr of the week. Give every child a role: one starts, another counts on their fingers, a third picks the new card. End with a light question: "When did you say Bismillah today?" This helps your child look back on their day and connect it with remembrance.

Make the weekly review a time for praise, not a test. Celebrate what your child mastered this week and move what they haven't learned yet to next week without blame. Within a few months you will notice adhkar becoming part of your family's everyday language, said as naturally as "please" and "thank you".

Common mistakes when teaching kids adhkar

  1. Too much at once: twenty adhkar in a week will all be forgotten. One dhikr learned well beats ten half-learned.
  2. Teaching unverified adhkar: social media is full of duas with specific numbers and rewards that have no basis. Stick to what is established in the books of Sunnah, and check when in doubt on a trusted source such as Hisn al-Muslim on Sunnah.com or the Dorar.net hadith encyclopedia.
  3. Memorizing without understanding: a child who understands the meaning says it with their heart. Always explain in a simple sentence.
  4. Constant fear: don't link adhkar only to fear of devils and the evil eye. Link them to love of Allah and gratitude too.
  5. Blaming them for forgetting: if your child forgets, remind them gently, or simply say it yourself out loud.
  6. Asking for what you don't do: a child who never hears their parents say "Bismillah" won't say it either.

Tools to support your child's adhkar routine

The Farhoon team is designing Islamic apps for children, coming soon, including a playful kids' adhkar routine with gentle motivation, an app for learning prayer with a friendly character, and a garden of good deeds. Until then, you can use the adhkar section in Rafiq Al-Taa. It is free, has no ads and needs no account, so your child can use it with you without seeing unsuitable content.

In short: start small, link every dhikr to a daily habit, explain the meaning and be the example. A child who grows up saying "Bismillah" at every beginning and "Alhamdulillah" for every blessing carries a seed that will grow with them for life.

faq.q: When should I start teaching my child duas?
faq.a: You can start from around age three with single words like 'Bismillah' and 'Alhamdulillah', simply by letting your child hear you say them in daily situations. From about six, most children can memorize full short adhkar, one per week. The key is to go gradually and link each dhikr to a situation that repeats every day.

faq.q: What is the easiest dua to start with?
faq.a: The easiest start is 'Bismillah' before eating and 'Alhamdulillah' after, because they are short and repeated several times a day. The Prophet ﷺ taught this to the young 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah, saying: 'Young boy, say Allah's name, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is in front of you' (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Then add the sneezing and bedtime adhkar.

faq.q: Do children need to read the full morning and evening adhkar?
faq.a: No. A child can begin with the short, authentic ones, such as Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq and An-Nas three times each, 'Bismillahil-ladhi la yadurru' three times, and 'Raditu billahi Rabba'. They can add more as they grow, until they are able to keep the full adhkar on their own when they are older.

faq.q: Are rewards for memorizing duas a good idea?
faq.a: Yes, simple rewards like stickers or stars help build the habit at the start. But they should be reduced gradually and always linked to meaning and love of Allah, so dhikr does not become just a way to earn a prize. Sincere praise and your own example have a much stronger long-term effect than gifts.

faq.q: How can I be sure the duas I teach are authentic?
faq.a: Rely on what is reported in well-known books of Sunnah, such as Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abi Dawud and Jami' at-Tirmidhi, and on Hisn al-Muslim. When in doubt, check on Sunnah.com or the Dorar.net hadith encyclopedia. Be cautious of viral messages that promise specific numbers and rewards without a source.

faq.q: What can my child say if they are afraid of the dark at bedtime?
faq.a: They can recite Ayat al-Kursi and the three Quls and say 'Bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya'. A parent can also say the words the Prophet ﷺ used for al-Hasan and al-Husayn: 'I seek protection for you in the perfect words of Allah from every devil, every poisonous creature and every harmful eye.' Then calmly reassure them that Allah protects them all night.
